sections.title: A skull in a Moroccan mine
sections.intro_md:
In 1961, miners digging for baryte in a limestone hill in western Morocco broke into an old cave filled with sediment. Out of the rubble came a human skull. For decades it was filed under Neanderthal-like oddities, about 40,000 years old. Then, in 2017, a team led by **Jean-Jacques Hublin** went back, found more bones and burnt flint, and dated the layer to about **315,000 years**. That pushed the oldest known *Homo sapiens* back by more than 100,000 years and moved it to the wrong corner of Africa: not the East African Rift, where textbooks put our cradle, but the far north-west.

That is the shape of this whole story. Every few years a bone, a tooth or a scrap of DNA forces a rewrite. The core still holds: our species arose in Africa and most of our ancestry outside Africa comes from one expansion about 50,000 years ago. Everything around that core keeps moving.

spotlights.name: The Jebel Irhoud fossils
spotlights.spot_it: A modern-looking face on a long, low, old-fashioned braincase.
spotlights.story_md: The Irhoud people had faces you could pass on a street: flat, tucked under the brain, with small brow ridges. Their braincases were different: long and low, not the round ball of a living human. That mismatch is the real lesson. Our face became modern first; the globe-shaped skull came later, perhaps as the brain itself reorganised. The 2017 date came from flint blades that had fallen into campfires, which resets their thermoluminescence clock, and a tooth gave a supporting 286,000 years. The site holds at least five people, including a child, among gazelle bones they had hunted and butchered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made Homo sapiens about 100,000 years older and showed our species was spread across Africa early.
spotlights.memory_hook: A modern face, an old head, and a Moroccan miner's shovel.

spotlights.name: A bush, not a ladder
spotlights.spot_it: Many human kinds alive at once, most of them dead ends.
spotlights.story_md: The old picture was a parade: a stooping ape becomes an upright man, one step at a time. The fossils show a bush. About 300,000 years ago, while early *Homo sapiens* lived in Morocco and Ethiopia, Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia, Denisovans across Asia, *Homo naledi* in South Africa and late *Homo erectus* in Java. Later came the tiny people of Flores and Luzon. For most of human history there was more than one kind of human on Earth. We are the only branch left, which makes our loneliness recent and unusual, not the normal state of things.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why we carry DNA from other humans: the branches met.
spotlights.memory_hook: Picture a hedge, not a staircase, and we are the last twig.

sections.title: The story in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Human origins is two stories braided together. The long one runs about **7 million years**, from the split with the chimpanzee line through dozens of upright apes and early humans. The short one runs about **300,000 years**, from the first *Homo sapiens* to now, and contains the expansion out of Africa that peopled every continent but Antarctica.

Three kinds of evidence carry it. **Fossils** show bodies. **Artefacts**, from stone tools to painted caves, show behaviour. **DNA**, from living people and from bones up to 400,000 years old, shows ancestry and mixing. When the three agree, the story is solid. When they disagree, as they often do on dates, you get the arguments you will meet all day.

Keep the eight numbers below in your head and the rest hangs off them.

spotlights.name: Our closest living cousin
spotlights.when: Split about 6 to 7 million years ago
spotlights.spot_it: Chimpanzees and bonobos: cousins, not grandparents.
spotlights.story_md: Humans did not descend from chimpanzees. Both lines descend from a shared ancestor that lived in Africa roughly 6 to 7 million years ago, and the chimp has been evolving for exactly as long as we have. Line our genomes up letter by letter and about 98.8% match, though counting insertions and deletions lowers that figure. The gap shows up in a few places that matter: brain growth, jaw muscles, hair, sweat glands, the shape of the pelvis. A chimp is better than you at short-term number memory and far stronger per kilogram. You are better at throwing, sweating and running long distances.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It fixes the most common misreading of evolution in one sentence.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chimps are your cousins, and your cousins are not your grandparents.

spotlights.name: Ninety-nine point nine per cent the same
spotlights.spot_it: Most human genetic difference sits inside populations, not between them.
spotlights.story_md: Any two people on Earth share about 99.9% of their DNA. Most of the remaining difference is found within any single population; only a small share separates continents. And most of the world's diversity sits in Africa, because humans lived there longest and only a subset left. Two people from neighbouring villages in Africa can be more different genetically than a Norwegian and a Japanese person. Chimpanzees from a single region of Africa carry more genetic diversity than all 8 billion humans, a sign that our species went through narrow bottlenecks and is young.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the hard evidence behind the claim that race is a poor biological category.
spotlights.memory_hook: One letter in a thousand, and most of it found next door.

sections.title: Seven million years in a few bones
sections.intro_md:
Before *Homo sapiens*, there were millions of years of upright apes and early humans, nearly all in Africa. The evidence is thin: a skull here, a footprint trail there, a skeleton that took decades to piece together. Each famous fossil has a nickname, a discoverer and usually a fight about what it means.

Three changes matter most. First, **walking upright**, which came early, at least 4 million years ago and perhaps 7. Second, **stone tools**, by about 3.3 million years ago. Third, the **genus Homo**, with bigger brains and longer legs, by about 2.8 million years ago, which soon walked out of Africa. Big brains came last, not first. That order surprised everyone, and it is part of why a fake fossil with a big brain and an ape jaw fooled Britain for 40 years.

spotlights.name: Toumaï
spotlights.spot_it: A crushed, chimp-sized skull with a heavy brow and small canine teeth.
spotlights.story_md: On 19 July 2001, a Chadian student, **Ahounta Djimdoumalbaye**, working with Michel Brunet's team, found a skull lying on the sand of the Djurab Desert. It was about 7 million years old, close to the date geneticists give for the human and chimp split. The local Daza name given to it, *Toumaï*, means roughly *hope of life*, a name given to babies born before the dry season. Its small canines and the forward position of the hole where the spinal cord enters the skull hint at upright walking. Whether it walked on two legs is still argued, partly over a thigh bone found with it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It may be the oldest member of the human line, and it was found 2,500 km west of the Rift Valley.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hope of life, found on the sand of Chad.

spotlights.name: Ardi
spotlights.spot_it: Upright on the ground, with a grasping big toe for climbing.
spotlights.story_md: Ardi, a female *Ardipithecus ramidus* from Aramis in Ethiopia's Middle Awash, took 15 years to publish. The bones were so fragile that they crumbled at a touch and had to be removed in plaster and digitally rebuilt. When the team led by **Tim White** presented her in 2009, she scrambled expectations. She stood about 1.2 metres and walked upright on the ground, but kept an opposable big toe, like a thumb on her foot, for gripping branches. She was not a chimp that learned to walk. She was something that had never existed in the textbooks: a part-time biped in a woodland.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed the last common ancestor need not have looked like a chimpanzee.
spotlights.memory_hook: A walker with a thumb on her foot.

spotlights.name: Lucy
spotlights.spot_it: About 40% of one small skeleton, knees and pelvis built for walking.
spotlights.story_md: **Donald Johanson** and **Tom Gray** spotted an arm bone in a gully at Hadar, Ethiopia. That night, as the camp celebrated, the Beatles song *Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds* played again and again, and the skeleton got its name. In Amharic she is *Dinkinesh*: you are marvellous. She stood about 1.1 metres tall, had a chimp-sized brain and walked upright. In 2016 a CT study argued her broken bones fit a fall from a tall tree, which would make the most famous upright walker a climber who died climbing. Other researchers think the cracks happened after death.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She proved upright walking came long before big brains.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Beatles song, a tree, and you are marvellous.

spotlights.name: The Laetoli footprints
spotlights.spot_it: A 27-metre trail of human-like footprints pressed into volcanic ash.
spotlights.story_md: In 1976, at Laetoli in Tanzania, members of **Mary Leakey**'s team were joking around, throwing dried elephant dung at each other. **Andrew Hill**, diving to dodge a throw, landed on a hard surface pocked with animal footprints. Two years later the team found a hominin trail: about 70 prints of two or three individuals walking side by side across ash from the Sadiman volcano, set like cement after light rain. The prints show a heel strike, an arch and a big toe in line with the others. Something walked like us 3.66 million years ago.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are behaviour, not bones: the oldest secure evidence of fully upright walking.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dung fight that found the oldest walk.

spotlights.name: The Taung Child

where.label: Taung, North West Province, South Africa

spotlights.spot_it: A small child's face fused to a natural stone cast of its brain.
spotlights.story_md: In 1924 the anatomist **Raymond Dart** was dressing for a friend's wedding in Johannesburg when two crates of rock from a lime quarry at Taung arrived. In one was a natural cast of a brain and, fitting into it, a child's face. He spent 73 days freeing it, reportedly with his wife's knitting needles. In 1925 he named *Australopithecus africanus* and said humans began in Africa. The British establishment scoffed for 20 years. In 2006, Lee Berger noticed puncture marks in the eye sockets that match those left by eagles on monkeys today. The child was probably killed by a large bird of prey.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first early human found in Africa and its story is a lesson in scientific prejudice.
spotlights.memory_hook: Knitting needles, a wedding suit and an eagle's talons.

spotlights.name: Turkana Boy
spotlights.when: About 1.5 to 1.6 million years ago; found 1984
spotlights.spot_it: A nearly complete tall, slim skeleton with long legs.
spotlights.story_md: In August 1984, **Kamoya Kimeu**, the most successful fossil hunter of his time, spotted a skull fragment near the Nariokotome river west of Lake Turkana, Kenya. Over several seasons the team recovered most of a skeleton of a *Homo erectus* youth who died aged roughly 8 to 12. He already stood about 1.5 to 1.6 metres and had the long legs, narrow hips and barrel chest of a body built for walking and running in heat. This was the first human with modern body proportions, and it is the body that soon carried our genus out of Africa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the body plan for long-distance walking was in place 1.5 million years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: A boy taller than his grandchildren's grandchildren's apes.

spotlights.name: The Dmanisi skulls
spotlights.when: About 1.8 million years ago; first finds 1991
spotlights.spot_it: Five small-brained skulls found under a medieval Georgian town.
spotlights.story_md: Archaeologists digging the ruins of a medieval town at Dmanisi in Georgia found animal bones beneath the cellars, then human ones. The five skulls, about 1.8 million years old, are the oldest humans known outside Africa. Their brains were small, about 550 to 780 cubic centimetres, which killed the idea that only big-brained humans could leave Africa. Skull 5, published in 2013, is so varied from the others that some scientists argue many named early *Homo* species are one variable species. One old individual had lost all but one tooth years before death and still survived.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They show humans left Africa far earlier, and with smaller brains, than once thought.
spotlights.memory_hook: Old bones under the cellars of a medieval town.

spotlights.name: The Acheulean handaxe
spotlights.when: From about 1.76 million to about 200,000 years ago
spotlights.spot_it: A teardrop of stone, flaked on both faces to a symmetrical edge.
spotlights.story_md: The handaxe is the most successful tool design in history. The oldest, from Kokiselei in Kenya, are about 1.76 million years old, and people made them for about 1.5 million years across Africa, Europe and Asia. Shaping one takes planning: you must see the axe inside the stone and remove flakes from both sides in the right order. Brain scans of modern knappers learning the skill light up regions linked to language and planning. India holds some of the oldest outside Africa: at Attirampakkam, near Chennai, handaxes have been dated to about 1.5 million years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the longest-lived technology humans have made, and India shares its early chapters.
spotlights.memory_hook: One shape, one and a half million years, no updates.

sections.title: How we know: rocks, clocks and DNA
sections.intro_md:
Every date in this story comes from a clock, and every clock has a range. **Radiocarbon** works only back to about 50,000 years, which is why the out-of-Africa period sits at the edge of what it can see. Older layers need **argon dating** of volcanic ash, **luminescence** (when a grain of sand or a flint was last heated or exposed to light), **uranium-series** dating of cave crusts, or **cosmogenic burial dating** of buried quartz. Each can be thrown off: uranium can leach, sediments can mix, ash layers can be miscorrelated.

Then came genetics. In 1987 a family tree of mitochondrial DNA pointed to Africa. In 2010 a Neanderthal genome showed that our ancestors had mated with them. Since then, ancient DNA has rewritten more of this story than fossils have, and its pioneer won a Nobel Prize.

spotlights.name: Mitochondrial Eve
spotlights.spot_it: The most recent woman from whom every living person descends through an unbroken line of mothers.
spotlights.story_md: Mitochondria, the power units of our cells, carry their own small DNA, passed only from mother to child. In 1987, **Rebecca Cann**, **Mark Stoneking** and **Allan Wilson** compared it in 147 people from around the world and built a family tree. Its root sat in Africa, about 200,000 years ago. Journalists called the ancestral woman *Mitochondrial Eve*, and *Newsweek* put an African Adam and Eve on its cover. She was not the only woman alive. She simply is the one whose maternal line happened never to break. Later estimates of her age range from about 100,000 to 230,000 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first genetic evidence for a recent African origin, and it shocked the field.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not the first woman, just the last common mother.

spotlights.name: Svante Pääbo
spotlights.spot_it: The Swedish geneticist who read the Neanderthal genome.
spotlights.story_md: As a PhD student in Uppsala in the early 1980s, **Svante Pääbo** secretly extracted DNA from Egyptian mummies in the evenings, not sure his supervisor would approve. He published in 1985. At the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig he built clean rooms where staff dress like surgeons, because a single sneeze carries more DNA than an old bone. In 1997 his team read Neanderthal mitochondrial DNA. In 2010 came a draft of the whole Neanderthal genome and then the Denisovans, a human group discovered from DNA alone. He won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, the same prize his father, Sune Bergström, had won in 1982.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He founded palaeogenomics, the field that now drives most discoveries in human origins.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mummy at midnight, a Neanderthal in the machine, two Nobels in one family.

spotlights.name: Denisova Cave and the pinky bone
spotlights.spot_it: A cave in Siberia's Altai Mountains where a new kind of human was found by DNA.
spotlights.story_md: Denisova Cave is named after an 18th-century hermit, Dionisij, said to have lived there. In 2008 Russian archaeologists recovered the tip of a little finger from a young girl. Sent to Leipzig, its DNA did not match humans or Neanderthals. The mitochondrial DNA split from ours about a million years ago, and the nuclear genome, published in December 2010, showed a sister group of Neanderthals. They were named **Denisovans** after the cave. For years the whole species was known from that fingertip, a few teeth and DNA in the cave's soil. Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans all used the cave at different times.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first time a human group was discovered from its genome, not its skeleton.
spotlights.memory_hook: A species named from a pinky.

sections.title: Becoming Homo sapiens in Africa
sections.intro_md:
No single place was the cradle. The fossils between about 315,000 and 160,000 years ago come from Morocco, Ethiopia, Kenya and South Africa, and they do not look identical. The best current model, often called **African multiregionalism**, sees our species forming across a patchwork of linked populations that split, adapted to different environments, and met again over hundreds of thousands of years. Genes flowed between them like water between ponds in a wet season.

Behaviour arrived in pieces too. Shellfish and red ochre by about 164,000 years ago. Shell beads and engraved patterns by about 75,000 years ago. The first known deliberate burial in Africa by about 78,000 years ago. There was no single *moment* when people became modern. There was a long, uneven assembly, spread across a continent.

visual.title: Where the early Homo sapiens evidence lies

spotlights.name: Omo I
spotlights.spot_it: A broken skull with the high, rounded vault of a modern human.
spotlights.story_md: In 1967, a team working for **Richard Leakey** collected skull pieces from the Kibish Formation along Ethiopia's Omo River, at a spot named Kamoya's Hominid Site after Kamoya Kimeu. For decades Omo I was dated to about 195,000 years. In 2022 a team traced a thick ash layer lying above the fossil to a huge eruption of the Shala volcano, 400 km away, and dated it to about **233,000 years**. Because the ash covers the skull, the skull must be older still. Unlike Jebel Irhoud, Omo I has a fully rounded, modern-looking braincase.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the oldest fossil that looks fully like us, head and face.
spotlights.memory_hook: The ash came from a volcano 400 km away and set the minimum age.

spotlights.name: The Herto skulls
spotlights.spot_it: Large modern skulls with cut marks and a polished child's cranium.
spotlights.story_md: In 1997, Tim White's team found three skulls at Herto in Ethiopia's Middle Awash, about 160,000 years old. They were named *Homo sapiens idaltu*, from the Afar word for *elder*. The surprise was what had been done to them. Cut marks showed the skulls were defleshed with stone tools after death, and a child's skull had a polished surface, as if handled for a long time. Some see a mortuary ritual, a way of keeping the dead close. Others are more cautious. Either way, someone in the Afar 160,000 years ago treated a dead child's head as something to keep.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is early evidence of special treatment of the dead.
spotlights.memory_hook: A child's skull worn smooth by living hands.

spotlights.name: Pinnacle Point

where.label: Pinnacle Point, Mossel Bay, South Africa

spotlights.spot_it: Sea caves in a cliff near Mossel Bay where people ate mussels during an ice age.
spotlights.story_md: Between about 195,000 and 125,000 years ago, Africa went through a long cold, dry phase. In cave 13B at Pinnacle Point, on South Africa's south coast, **Curtis Marean**'s team found that by about 164,000 years ago people were collecting shellfish, grinding red ochre and making small bladelets. It is the oldest known seafood diet. Marean argues the Cape coast, with its rich intertidal zone and many edible bulbs inland, may have been a refuge that kept a small population going. Nearby, later layers show people heating stone in fires to make it easier to flake, a piece of engineering.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows coastal living, pigment and planning far earlier than the European record.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mussels and ochre in an ice age: the oldest beach diet.

spotlights.name: Blombos Cave

where.label: Blombos Cave, Western Cape, South Africa

spotlights.spot_it: A small cave on the Cape coast with engraved ochre, shell beads and the oldest drawing.
spotlights.story_md: **Christopher Henshilwood** first dug Blombos Cave in the 1990s, on land near his grandfather's holiday cottage. It has given archaeology some of its oldest symbols: pieces of red ochre engraved with crosshatched lines about 75,000 years ago, beads made of tiny *Nassarius* shells, pierced and worn, and a 100,000-year-old paint kit mixed in abalone shells. In 2018 the team reported a flake of stone with nine red lines drawn in a crosshatch with an ochre crayon, about 73,000 years old. It is the oldest known drawing, older than the European cave paintings by more than 30,000 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows symbolic behaviour, not just survival skills, in Africa long before Europe.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hashtag drawn in crayon 73,000 years ago.

spotlights.name: Mtoto, the oldest burial in Africa

where.label: Panga ya Saidi, Kilifi County, Kenya

spotlights.spot_it: A small child laid on its side in a pit, knees drawn up.
spotlights.story_md: In the cave of Panga ya Saidi, near the Kenyan coast, excavators found a pit with a tightly packed cluster of bones. Lab work in Spain revealed a child aged about two and a half to three, about 78,000 years old, laid on its right side with knees to chest. The skull had slumped in a way that suggests it rested on a pillow of something perishable, and the body may have been wrapped. The researchers named the child **Mtoto**, Swahili for *child*. It is the oldest known deliberate human burial in Africa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows people in Africa burying their dead with care by 78,000 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mtoto: a child laid down on a pillow 78,000 years ago.

sections.title: The exits that failed
sections.intro_md:
The out-of-Africa story has a prologue that textbooks used to leave out. *Homo sapiens* walked out of Africa more than once before the expansion that stuck. Fossils in Israel and Greece, and stone tools and a finger bone in Arabia, show early modern humans beyond Africa from perhaps 210,000 to 85,000 years ago.

These early pioneers mostly left no living descendants. In the Levant, Neanderthals reoccupied the same caves after them. The likely reason is climate. During wet phases, the Sahara and Arabia turned green, with lakes and rivers, opening corridors. When they dried, groups were stranded or shrank. Africa leaked people outward in pulses, and most pulses fizzled. Genetics hints that a little of their DNA may survive, absorbed into Neanderthals, but that is still argued.

spotlights.name: The Misliya jaw
spotlights.spot_it: An upper jaw with teeth from a collapsed cave on Mount Carmel.
spotlights.story_md: In 2002 a first-year student at Tel Aviv University, digging at Misliya Cave on the slopes of Mount Carmel, Israel, found a left upper jaw with eight teeth. In 2018 the team led by **Israel Hershkovitz** dated it to 177,000 to 194,000 years and called it the oldest modern human outside Africa. Critics replied in the same journal that the uranium-series dates might be flawed, allowing an age as young as 60,000 to 70,000 years. The jaw sits in a layer with Levallois stone tools, a technique that needs careful planning.
spotlights.why_it_matters: If the date holds, our species was knocking on Asia's door around 185,000 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: A student's first dig, a jaw, and an argument about uranium.

spotlights.name: Apidima 1
spotlights.spot_it: A broken back of a skull, rounded like ours, from a seaside cave in Greece.
spotlights.story_md: Two battered skulls came out of Apidima Cave in Greece's Mani peninsula in the late 1970s and sat in a museum for 40 years. In 2019 **Katerina Harvati**'s team scanned and virtually rebuilt them. Apidima 2 looked Neanderthal and dated to more than 170,000 years. Apidima 1, just the back of a braincase, was rounded like a modern human's and dated to more than 210,000 years, which would make it the oldest *Homo sapiens* outside Africa by a wide margin. Many experts think the piece is too incomplete to say. It remains a strong claim, not a settled fact.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It suggests modern humans reached Europe and then vanished, long before the main arrival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two skulls in one cave: a sapiens, then a Neanderthal.

spotlights.name: Skhul and Qafzeh
spotlights.spot_it: Early modern humans buried in caves in Israel, one child with deer antlers on its chest.
spotlights.story_md: In the 1930s, at Skhul on Mount Carmel, and later at Qafzeh near Nazareth, excavators found the remains of more than two dozen early modern humans. They are among the oldest deliberate burials anywhere. At Qafzeh, a child known as Qafzeh 11 lies with the antlers of a red deer placed across its chest, hands clasping them. Seashells pierced and stained with ochre were carried there from the coast, about 35 km away. Then the record changes. After about 80,000 years ago, Neanderthals hold the region, and these early sapiens left no clear descendants.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the best-known of the early exits and show that being modern was not enough to win.
spotlights.memory_hook: Antlers in a child's arms, 100,000 years ago.

sections.title: The one that worked: about 50,000 years ago
sections.intro_md:
Here is the core of the story. Almost everyone alive outside Africa today descends mainly from a population that left Africa, probably through north-east Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, sometime around **60,000 to 50,000 years ago**. Genetics now dates the Neanderthal mixing that all non-Africans share to about **50,500 to 43,500 years ago**, and the expansion across Eurasia followed fast.

Two routes are argued over. A **northern route** through Sinai into the Levant, and a **southern route** across the Bab-el-Mandeb strait into Yemen and along the coasts of Arabia and India. Both may have been used. Within about 10,000 years, people had reached Australia, which required crossing open sea, and Europe, where they met Neanderthals face to face. Some of those first Europeans died out without descendants. Expansion was not a march. It was a series of bold, often failed, family-sized ventures.

spotlights.name: Bab-el-Mandeb, the Gate of Grief
spotlights.spot_it: The narrow strait between the Horn of Africa and Yemen, today about 30 km of water.
spotlights.story_md: The name means *Gate of Grief* in Arabic, for the ships it wrecked. During ice ages, so much water was locked in ice sheets that sea level fell by up to about 70 metres or more, narrowing the strait and exposing islands, so a crossing could be made in short hops by raft or swimming. If the southern route is right, a small group crossed here, perhaps a few hundred people at most, and followed the coast east, eating shellfish. A few hundred people carrying a fraction of Africa's genetic diversity is one reason all non-Africans are so genetically similar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the leading candidate for the doorway through which most of humanity's ancestors walked.
spotlights.memory_hook: Through the Gate of Grief on a low tide of the Ice Age.

spotlights.name: Toba, the super-eruption
spotlights.spot_it: A 100-km lake in Sumatra filling the crater of the largest eruption of the last 2 million years.
spotlights.story_md: About 74,000 years ago the Toba volcano in Sumatra blew out thousands of cubic kilometres of rock and ash, leaving a crater now filled by Lake Toba, about 100 km long, with an island nearly the size of Singapore in the middle. Ash fell as far as India. In 1998 the anthropologist **Stanley Ambrose** proposed that the volcanic winter nearly wiped out humanity, causing a genetic bottleneck. The evidence has since turned against him. Tools in India continue across the ash layer, and at Pinnacle Point in South Africa microscopic Toba glass sits in layers where people kept thriving.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a classic case of a dramatic theory that the evidence did not support.
spotlights.memory_hook: The volcano that did not quite end us.

spotlights.name: Madjedbebe
spotlights.spot_it: A sandstone rock shelter in Arnhem Land holding Australia's oldest dated tools.
spotlights.story_md: Madjedbebe lies on the country of the **Mirarr** people, surrounded by a uranium lease. The Mirarr agreed to the 2015 excavation on terms that gave them control over the site and its findings. Dating published in 2017 put the earliest layer at about **65,000 years**, with grinding stones, ground ochre and the world's oldest edge-ground axe heads. Reaching Australia meant at least one open-sea crossing of tens of kilometres, even at low sea level. Critics argue artefacts may have sunk into older sand, and that 50,000 years is the safer minimum. Either date makes Aboriginal Australians the world's oldest continuous cultures.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It sets the deepest date for humans in Australia and for open-sea voyaging.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixty-five thousand years of ochre in one rock shelter.

spotlights.name: Lake Mungo

where.label: Lake Mungo, Mungo National Park, New South Wales

spotlights.spot_it: A dry lake bed in New South Wales with eroded white dunes called the Walls of China.
spotlights.story_md: In 1968 the geologist **Jim Bowler** noticed burnt bones eroding from a dune at Lake Mungo. They were the remains of a young woman, cremated, smashed and burnt again: the oldest known cremation in the world. In 1974 Bowler found a man laid on his back with hands clasped, sprinkled with red ochre that had been carried from far away. Both are about 42,000 years old. After long campaigns by Aboriginal elders, Mungo Lady was returned in 1992, and in 2017 Mungo Man came home to country in a vintage hearse, driven slowly across the outback.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows complex burial rites in Australia as old as any in Europe.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's oldest cremation, and a hearse driving home 42,000 years later.

spotlights.name: The Ranis and Zlatý kůň family
spotlights.spot_it: Distant relatives buried 230 km apart, from a lineage that died out.
spotlights.story_md: Under a castle at Ranis in Germany lies a cave called the Ilsenhöhle, where bones about 45,000 years old were dug up in the 1930s. In 2024, genomes from six of them revealed a family group, including a mother and her child. Even more startling, they were distant kin of a woman whose skull was found in 1950 in Zlatý kůň cave in Czechia, 230 km away. Their population was tiny and isolated, the deepest known branch of the out-of-Africa family, and it left no descendants. Their Neanderthal DNA came from the same mixing event as everyone else's, dated to about 45,000 to 49,000 years ago.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They pinned down when the Neanderthal mixing happened, using a family tree that ended.
spotlights.memory_hook: A family across 230 km of Ice Age Europe, with no descendants today.

sections.title: The other humans
sections.intro_md:
When our ancestors spread out, the world was not empty. **Neanderthals** had lived in Europe and western Asia for over 300,000 years. **Denisovans** ranged across Asia, from Siberia to Tibet to China, and probably into South-East Asia. On islands lived small, strange humans: *Homo floresiensis* on Flores and *Homo luzonensis* on Luzon. In South Africa, *Homo naledi* survived until at least about 236,000 years ago.

Within about 10,000 years of our arrival in Europe, the Neanderthals were gone, by about 40,000 years ago. Why is still argued: competition, small numbers, inbreeding, climate swings, disease, and absorption into our larger population all play a part. They were not simple brutes. They buried some of their dead, cared for the injured, made pigments and jewellery, and some of their genes live inside you.

data.where: Siberia, Tibet, China, probably South-East Asia
data.known_from: Finger, teeth, jaws, Harbin skull, genomes

data.when: At least about 50,000 to 67,000 years ago

spotlights.name: Neanderthal 1
spotlights.spot_it: A thick, low skull cap with a heavy double-arched brow ridge.
spotlights.story_md: In August 1856, quarry workers clearing the Feldhofer cave in the Neander valley near Düsseldorf threw out a skull cap and bones. A local schoolteacher, **Johann Carl Fuhlrott**, saw they were not a bear's. In 1864 the anatomist William King named *Homo neanderthalensis*, the first extinct human species ever named. The valley itself was named after a 17th-century hymn writer, Joachim Neander, whose surname was a Greek version of *Neumann*: new man. The cave was quarried away, but in 1997 to 2000 researchers found its old spoil heaps and pulled out bone fragments that fit the original skeleton. The first Neanderthal DNA came from this same bone in 1997.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It began the science of human evolution, three years before Darwin's Origin of Species.
spotlights.memory_hook: The valley of the new man held the first old human.

spotlights.name: Shanidar Cave
spotlights.spot_it: A vast cave mouth in the Zagros Mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan.
spotlights.story_md: Between 1951 and 1960 **Ralph Solecki** recovered ten Neanderthals from Shanidar Cave. One man, Shanidar 1, had a withered right arm, a crushed left eye socket, probable deafness and a damaged leg, yet lived into his 40s, which means others fed and protected him. Another, Shanidar 4, was famous as the *flower burial* because pollen clusters lay around the body; burrowing rodents are now the likelier explanation. Since 2014 a new team has worked the cave, and in 2018 it found Shanidar Z, a woman about 75,000 years old, whose flattened skull was pieced together and her face rebuilt in 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It holds the strongest evidence that Neanderthals cared for the injured.
spotlights.memory_hook: A one-armed, half-blind, deaf man who was kept alive.

spotlights.name: The Harbin skull: a Denisovan face
spotlights.spot_it: A huge, nearly complete skull with a massive brow and a big brain.
spotlights.story_md: The story told is that in 1933 a labourer building a railway bridge in Harbin, north-east China, found a skull and hid it in a well to keep it from the Japanese-run authorities. In 2018 his family handed it to scientists. In 2021 it was named *Homo longi*, Dragon Man, after the Black Dragon River region. It has a brain as large as ours, around 1,420 cubic centimetres, a heavy brow and enormous molars. In June 2025, two studies settled its identity: 95 proteins from the bone and mitochondrial DNA from plaque on its one remaining tooth matched Denisovans. For the first time, we know what a Denisovan looked like.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gave the Denisovans a face after 15 years as a genome without a body.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hidden in a well for 85 years, and the plaque on its tooth told who it was.

spotlights.name: The Hobbit of Flores
spotlights.when: Bones about 100,000 to 60,000 years ago; found 2003
spotlights.spot_it: A grown woman about 1.06 metres tall with a brain the size of a chimp's.
spotlights.story_md: In 2003, an Indonesian and Australian team digging in Liang Bua cave on Flores found the skeleton of an adult about 1.06 metres tall, with a brain of about 426 cubic centimetres. Named *Homo floresiensis* in 2004, she was nicknamed the hobbit. Sceptics said she was a modern human with a disease; more skeletons and a study of her wrists and feet buried that idea. First dated to as recent as 12,000 years, the bones were redated in 2016 to about 100,000 to 60,000 years. Her ancestors reached Flores by at least 700,000 years ago, and on the island, they shrank.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed small-brained humans survived until our own species was spreading.
spotlights.memory_hook: A metre tall, a chimp-sized brain, and stone tools.

spotlights.name: Homo luzonensis
spotlights.when: At least about 50,000 to 67,000 years ago; named 2019
spotlights.spot_it: Small teeth and curved finger and toe bones from a Philippine cave.
spotlights.story_md: In 2007 a toe bone from Callao Cave on Luzon in the Philippines was dated to about 67,000 years. Further digging produced teeth and finger and toe bones from at least three individuals, and in 2019 they were named a new species, *Homo luzonensis*. Its teeth are small and simple, like ours, but its curved finger and toe bones look like those of *Australopithecus*, 2 million years older. Luzon was never joined to mainland Asia by land, so its ancestors crossed water somehow. A butchered rhinoceros on the island hints that humans were there by about 700,000 years ago.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a second island human, proof that Flores was not a one-off.
spotlights.memory_hook: Modern teeth, ancient toes, an island no one could walk to.

spotlights.name: Homo naledi

where.label: Rising Star Cave, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa

spotlights.spot_it: A small-brained human with modern-looking hands and feet, found deep in a cave.
spotlights.story_md: In September 2013, two cavers squeezed through a gap just 18 cm wide in South Africa's Rising Star cave system and found bones scattered on a chamber floor. **Lee Berger** recruited slim scientists, nicknamed the underground astronauts, to retrieve them. They brought out more than 1,500 pieces from at least 15 individuals, the richest hominin find in Africa. *Homo naledi* had a brain of only about 465 to 610 cubic centimetres but lived as recently as about 236,000 years ago, alongside early *Homo sapiens*. Berger's later claims that naledi buried its dead and carved symbols have been fiercely disputed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proves small brains survived alongside our own species in Africa.
spotlights.memory_hook: An 18-centimetre squeeze to reach a small-brained cousin.

sections.title: The cousins inside us
sections.intro_md:
In 2010 the draft Neanderthal genome answered a question fossil experts had argued about for a century: did our ancestors mate with Neanderthals? Yes. Everyone with ancestry from outside Africa carries roughly **2%** Neanderthal DNA. Many people in Papua New Guinea, Australia and the Philippines also carry several per cent of **Denisovan** DNA. Even many Africans carry a small amount of Neanderthal DNA, brought back by later migrations into Africa.

The fragments are not evenly spread. Natural selection cleared Neanderthal DNA from some regions of the genome, such as the X chromosome and genes active in the testes, which hints that hybrid males may have had reduced fertility. In other places it kept and spread useful variants for immunity, skin and altitude. Put together all the Neanderthal pieces carried by living people and you recover a large part of the Neanderthal genome.

visual.title: Archaic DNA in living people (approximate per cent of genome)

spotlights.name: Oase 1, the man with a Neanderthal great-great-grandparent
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy modern human jaw from a Romanian cave of bones.
spotlights.story_md: In 2002, cavers exploring Peștera cu Oase, the Cave with Bones, in south-western Romania found a human jaw on the surface. It is one of Europe's oldest modern humans, 37,000 to 42,000 years old. In 2015 its DNA revealed 6 to 9% Neanderthal ancestry, more than anyone sequenced before or since. Three stretches of Neanderthal DNA were so long that they could not have been broken up by many generations of shuffling. This man had a Neanderthal ancestor just four to six generations back. His people left no detectable descendants in later Europe.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the closest direct evidence of a mixed family in Europe.
spotlights.memory_hook: His great-great-great-grandparent was a Neanderthal.

spotlights.name: Denny, the hybrid girl
spotlights.spot_it: A thumbnail-sized bone from a teenage girl with a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.
spotlights.story_md: In 2012, archaeologists at Denisova Cave had thousands of bone scraps too small to identify. A team at Oxford ran them through a protein test called ZooMS and found one human piece, about 2 cm long. Its genome, published in August 2018 by **Viviane Slon** and Svante Pääbo, belonged to a girl at least 13 years old. Her mother was Neanderthal, her father Denisovan. She is a first-generation hybrid. Her father himself had a Neanderthal ancestor further back. Finding one first-generation hybrid among the very few ancient genomes sequenced suggests these groups mixed often when they met.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the only first-generation offspring of two different human groups ever identified.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mother from one human kind, a father from another, and a bone as long as a thumbnail.

spotlights.name: The Tibetan altitude gene
spotlights.when: Selected in the last several thousand years; found 2014
spotlights.spot_it: Highlanders who thrive at 4,000 metres without overproducing red blood cells.
spotlights.story_md: Most people who move to high altitude make extra haemoglobin, which thickens the blood and can cause heart trouble. Tibetans do not, and much of that is down to a version of a gene called **EPAS1**. In 2014 a team showed the Tibetan version of EPAS1 came from Denisovans or their close relatives: it exists only in Denisovans, in Tibetans and at low frequency in Han Chinese. In 2019 a Denisovan jaw was identified from Baishiya Karst Cave, 3,280 metres up on the Tibetan Plateau, about 160,000 years old. The Denisovans had lived at altitude long before.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest example of a borrowed gene helping living people survive.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tibetans breathe thin air with a Denisovan gene.

spotlights.name: The Neanderthal COVID risk
spotlights.spot_it: A Neanderthal stretch of chromosome 3 linked to severe COVID-19.
spotlights.story_md: In 2020, as hospitals filled, a study of 3,199 hospitalised patients found that a gene cluster on chromosome 3 was the biggest genetic risk factor for severe COVID-19. **Hugo Zeberg** and **Svante Pääbo** showed the risky version was a block of about 50,000 DNA letters inherited from Neanderthals. It is carried by about **50% of people in South Asia** and about 16% in Europe, but is almost absent in East Asia. It is most common in Bangladesh. A follow-up study in 2021 found a different Neanderthal variant, on chromosome 12, that slightly protects against severe disease.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made Neanderthal ancestry a medical question for South Asia in particular.
spotlights.memory_hook: A gift from a Neanderthal 50,000 years ago turned up in a COVID ward in 2020.

sections.title: Minds that made marks
sections.intro_md:
For most of the 20th century, the story was that modern minds switched on in Europe about 40,000 years ago in a *creative explosion*: the painted caves of France, carved figurines in Germany. That story has collapsed. Engraved ochre and shell beads in Africa are 75,000 to 100,000 years old. And the oldest dated cave art in the world is in **Indonesia**, on the island of Sulawesi.

In 2024 a scene of human-like figures and a pig in Sulawesi was dated to at least 51,200 years ago. In January 2026 a hand stencil on nearby Muna Island was dated to at least 67,800 years ago. If those dates hold, the people who first crossed toward Australia were already making images on cave walls. Meanwhile, some marks in Spanish caves have been attributed to Neanderthals. The line between us and them in art is blurring too.

spotlights.name: The warty pigs of Sulawesi
spotlights.spot_it: Red and mulberry pigs painted on limestone, with hand stencils hovering nearby.
spotlights.story_md: In the limestone karsts of Maros-Pangkep in South Sulawesi, cave walls carry paintings of the local warty pig, *Sus celebensis*. In 2017, the Indonesian archaeologist **Basran Burhan** found a life-size pig, 136 cm long, in Leang Tedongnge, a cave reachable only in the dry season; dated through the calcite crust on top, it is at least 45,500 years old. In 2024 a new method, laser-ablation uranium-series imaging, dated a scene in Leang Karampuang showing three human-like figures interacting with a pig to at least **51,200 years** ago. It is the oldest known storytelling picture.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It moved the oldest figurative art and the oldest visual story from Europe to Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pigs, not bison: the first great painters lived in Sulawesi.

spotlights.name: The Muna hand stencil
spotlights.when: At least 67,800 years ago; published January 2026
spotlights.spot_it: A faint negative hand, made by blowing pigment around a hand pressed to the rock.
spotlights.story_md: On Muna Island, off south-east Sulawesi, the cave of Liang Metanduno carries stencils of human hands under later paintings. The archaeologist **Adhi Agus Oktaviana** first explored it in 2015. In January 2026, his team reported that a thin calcite crust over one stencil dated to about 71,600 years, giving the hand a minimum age of **67,800 years**. That is 1,100 years older than the oldest hand stencil in Spain, attributed to Neanderthals. One stencil shows a pointing finger. Some researchers warn that uranium leaching can inflate such dates, so the record may be revised.
spotlights.why_it_matters: If it holds, it is the oldest known rock art made by our species.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hand on a wall, at least 67,800 years old.

spotlights.name: The Lion Man
spotlights.spot_it: A standing figure with a lion's head and a human body, 31 cm tall, carved in mammoth ivory.
spotlights.story_md: On 25 August 1939, a week before the Second World War began, excavators in the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in southern Germany found hundreds of ivory fragments. The dig was abandoned and the pieces sat in boxes for 30 years. In 1969 **Joachim Hahn** fitted them into a figure: a human body with a cave lion's head. More fragments found in 2009 to 2013 were added in a new restoration. Experiments with flint tools suggest carving it took about 400 hours. It is the oldest known depiction of a being that does not exist, a creature of the imagination.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is early evidence of myth: thinking about things that are not there.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four hundred hours of carving for a creature no one had ever seen.

spotlights.name: The Venus of Hohle Fels and the vulture-bone flute
spotlights.when: At least 35,000 to 40,000 years ago; found 2008
spotlights.spot_it: A 6 cm ivory woman with a loop for a head, worn as a pendant.
spotlights.story_md: In September 2008, **Nicholas Conard**'s team in Hohle Fels cave, Germany, found six pieces of a mammoth-ivory figurine. Reassembled, the 6 cm figure shows a woman with huge breasts and exaggerated hips and no head: in its place is a carved loop, so it could be hung on a cord. It is the oldest undisputed depiction of a human being. Metres away the team found a flute made from the wing bone of a griffon vulture, with five finger holes, also about 35,000 to 40,000 years old and among the oldest known musical instruments.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows sculpture, ornament and music together in one Ice Age cave.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pendant woman and a vulture flute in the same layer.

spotlights.name: Chauvet Cave
spotlights.spot_it: Charcoal lions, rhinos and horses drawn with shading and movement.
spotlights.story_md: On 18 December 1994, three cavers, **Jean-Marie Chauvet**, Éliette Brunel and Christian Hillaire, felt a draught from a rubble pile in the Ardèche gorge in France, cleared it and found a sealed cave. Inside were hundreds of images, including lions, woolly rhinos and a panel of four horses' heads drawn with shading. Radiocarbon dates put the oldest at about 36,000 years. The cave is closed to protect it; a full-scale replica, the Caverne du Pont d'Arc, opened in 2015. Cave bear skulls and footprints still lie on the floor.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that the earliest European cave art was already sophisticated, not crude.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lions drawn in charcoal 36,000 years ago, still sharp today.

compare.difference: Lascaux, about 17,000 years old, is painted in colour; Chauvet is about twice as old and mostly drawn in charcoal and red ochre.

sections.title: India's part in the story
sections.intro_md:
India sits on the most likely route from Africa to Australia, and its record is long and puzzling. Handaxes near Chennai go back about **1.5 million years**. Advanced Middle Palaeolithic tools at the same site appear about **385,000 years** ago, long before most dates for *Homo sapiens* in Asia. Ash from the Toba eruption, 74,000 years ago, lies across sites in Andhra Pradesh with tools above and below it. Yet India has only one important hominin fossil from this period, a skull cap from the Narmada valley, because acidic soils and monsoon rivers destroy bones.

Genetics fills the gap. A 2025 study of 2,762 Indian genomes found that most of India's genetic variation traces to the single out-of-Africa expansion about 50,000 years ago, followed by mixing with Neanderthals and Denisovans. Indians also carry more distinct Neanderthal segments than any other population studied. Later layers came from Iranian-related farmers and steppe pastoralists.

spotlights.name: Attirampakkam
spotlights.spot_it: A river-side site near Chennai with thousands of handaxes and flakes.
spotlights.story_md: In 1863 the geologist **Robert Bruce Foote** picked up a handaxe at Pallavaram, near Madras: the first Palaeolithic tool recognised in India. Nearby Attirampakkam, on the Kortallaiyar river about 60 km from Chennai, has been dug since 1999 by **Shanti Pappu** and Kumar Akhilesh. In 2011 they dated handaxes there to about 1.5 million years, among the oldest outside Africa. In 2018 they reported Levallois tools, a more advanced technique, from about 385,000 years ago. Either *Homo sapiens* left Africa far earlier than thought, or older humans developed the method in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's strongest claim to a central role in the deep human story.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chennai's suburbs hold tools older than the human species.

spotlights.name: The Narmada skull
spotlights.when: About 160,000 to 50,000 years ago; found 5 December 1982
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy skull cap from the north bank of the Narmada river.
spotlights.story_md: On 5 December 1982, **Arun Sonakia** of the Geological Survey of India found a skull cap lying on the surface of a gravel bank near Hathnora in Madhya Pradesh. It remains the only significant early human fossil from India. First described as a man and as *Homo erectus*, it was later identified as a woman in her 30s, and the name changed from Narmada Man to Narmada Human. Experts have called it *Homo erectus*, archaic *Homo sapiens* and *Homo heidelbergensis*. Its age is uncertain, somewhere between about 160,000 and 50,000 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's only early human face from the deep past, and nobody agrees what it is.
spotlights.memory_hook: One skull, four species names, no consensus.

spotlights.name: Jwalapuram and the Toba ash
spotlights.spot_it: A valley in Andhra Pradesh where a thick white layer of volcanic ash cuts through the soil.
spotlights.story_md: In the Jurreru river valley in Andhra Pradesh, a white layer of ash from Toba, 3,000 km away in Sumatra, lies up to a few metres thick. In 2007 **Michael Petraglia**, working with Indian colleagues including Ravi Korisettar, reported stone tools both below and above the ash. They looked similar to African tools made by *Homo sapiens*, so the team argued modern humans were in India before the eruption and survived it. Critics say the tools could be the work of other humans. The site's name, fittingly, means *city of fire* in Telugu.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the main evidence that Toba did not wipe out India's people.
spotlights.memory_hook: City of fire, under ash from a volcano 3,000 km away.

spotlights.name: Bhimbetka rock shelters
spotlights.when: Paintings from about 10,000 years ago to historic times
spotlights.spot_it: Sandstone overhangs in Madhya Pradesh painted with hunters, dancers and animals in red and white.
spotlights.story_md: In 1957 the archaeologist **V. S. Wakankar** saw rock formations from a train window near Bhopal that reminded him of shelters he had seen in Spain and France. He got off and found a cluster of about 750 rock shelters, roughly 500 of them painted. The oldest paintings, of bison, deer and hunters, are thought to be Mesolithic, roughly 10,000 years old, and the site shows human use going back much further. Bhimbetka became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. In 2021, a reported fossil of the ancient animal *Dickinsonia* there turned out, in 2023, to be the imprint of a decayed beehive.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's largest gallery of prehistoric art.
spotlights.memory_hook: A view from a train window became a World Heritage Site.

spotlights.name: The Andaman Islanders
spotlights.when: Living communities; deep ancestry from the early dispersal
spotlights.spot_it: Small Indigenous communities whose ancestry branches deep from the first Asians.
spotlights.story_md: The Andaman Islands hold some of the most isolated people on Earth: the Onge, the Jarawa, the Great Andamanese and the Sentinelese, who refuse outside contact. Genetic studies, including a 2005 *Science* paper by Indian scientists, found maternal lineages found nowhere else, branching from the earliest out-of-Africa expansion along the coast. Their ancestry is related to that of other Asians and Oceanians, and they serve as a rough stand-in for the ancient South Asian hunter-gatherers whose DNA all Indians carry. Their numbers are tiny: a few hundred Jarawa and about a hundred Onge. Their protection is a matter of law and survival.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are a living link to the first wave of humans to reach South Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: On small islands, a very old branch of the human family tree.

spotlights.name: India's 50,000-year genetic history
spotlights.spot_it: Three ancestral streams in almost every Indian, on top of one African exit.
spotlights.story_md: In 2025, a team led by **Priya Moorjani** published 2,762 whole genomes from across India. Most Indians, it found, carry ancestry from three main sources: ancient South Asian hunter-gatherers, Iranian-related Neolithic farmers, and Eurasian steppe pastoralists who arrived later. Underneath, most variation traces to a single out-of-Africa expansion about 50,000 years ago, plus 1 to 2% from Neanderthals and Denisovans. Indians carry the largest variety of Neanderthal segments of any population. Endogamy, marrying within caste or community over thousands of years, created strong founder effects, which raise the risk of some recessive diseases.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns ancient history into a medical map for 1.4 billion people.
spotlights.memory_hook: One African exit, three streams, and endogamy written in the genome.

sections.title: Filling the map
sections.intro_md:
After about 50,000 years ago, humans spread to nearly every habitable place, in a sequence written in stone tools, bones and genes. South and East Asia and Australia came first, then Europe and Central Asia. Siberia's Arctic followed. The Americas were reached at least about 21,000 years ago, and the remote Pacific only within the last 3,000 years, by Polynesian voyagers who found New Zealand about 750 years ago.

As people spread, their bodies adapted. Lighter skin spread in northern Europe much later than once thought, partly over the last 8,000 years. The ability to digest milk as adults spread with herding. Short, stocky builds in the Arctic and tall, slim builds in hot savannah fit old rules of heat loss. None of these changes split humans into separate kinds. They are small adjustments laid over one recently shared body plan.

spotlights.name: The White Sands footprints

where.label: White Sands National Park, New Mexico, USA

spotlights.spot_it: Human footprints, many of them children's, in the gypsum of an ancient lake shore.
spotlights.story_md: In New Mexico's White Sands National Park, footprints of ice-age animals and people appear on the surface of a dried lake when the soil moisture is just right; locals call them ghost tracks. In 2021, a team led by Matthew Bennett dated seeds in layers above and below human prints to between about 23,000 and 21,000 years ago, at the height of the last ice age. Critics worried the seeds of a water plant could give falsely old dates. In 2023, pollen and luminescence dates agreed. Most of the prints were made by teenagers and children, walking near mammoths and giant ground sloths.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They push humans in the Americas back by about 7,000 years beyond older models.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ghost tracks of teenagers beside the mammoths.

spotlights.name: Beringia, the lost land bridge
spotlights.when: Exposed during the last ice age, flooded about 11,000 years ago
spotlights.spot_it: A vanished subcontinent, up to 1,000 km wide, joining Siberia and Alaska.
spotlights.story_md: During the last ice age, sea level was about 120 metres lower and a wide plain of grassland and tundra joined Siberia to Alaska. Today it lies under the shallow Bering and Chukchi seas, and the Bering Strait is about 82 km wide. Genetic evidence suggests ancestors of Native Americans may have lived in Beringia for thousands of years, cut off by ice sheets, before moving south, perhaps along the Pacific coast by boat. When the ice melted, the land bridge drowned. The Americas were reached by people walking, sailing or both, across a land that no longer exists.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains how the last continents were reached on foot.
spotlights.memory_hook: A country the size of a subcontinent, now under the sea.

spotlights.name: How skin colour changed
spotlights.when: Mostly within the last 40,000 years, much of it within 8,000
spotlights.spot_it: Gene variants such as SLC24A5 and SLC45A2 that lighten skin.
spotlights.story_md: The first modern humans out of Africa almost certainly had dark skin, which protects folate in the blood from strong ultraviolet light. In regions with weak sunlight, lighter skin helps the body make vitamin D. Ancient DNA shows the main European light-skin variants, in genes such as **SLC24A5**, spread widely only with farming over the last 8,000 years or so; a 10,000-year-old Briton, Cheddar Man, probably had dark skin and blue eyes. The same SLC24A5 variant is also common in South Asia, especially in the north-west. Light skin evolved more than once, in East Asia through different genes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows skin colour is a recent, local adaptation, not a deep division.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dark skin first, light skin late, and more than once.

sections.title: Myths and misreadings
sections.intro_md:
Human origins attracts myths, because it is about us. Some are old scientific mistakes that live on in popular culture, like the stooping Neanderthal brute. Some are misreadings of real results, like the idea that Mitochondrial Eve was the only woman alive. One is an outright fraud that fooled the British establishment for four decades.

The most important misreading is the idea of a *missing link*, one fossil halfway between ape and human. There is no single link. There are thousands of fossils from dozens of species, a continuum with many side branches. Another is that out of Africa means *everyone else is descended from Africans who left, and Africans stayed the same*. Africans have evolved for exactly as long as everyone else, and Africa today holds more human genetic diversity than the rest of the world combined.

spotlights.name: Piltdown Man
spotlights.spot_it: A human skull and an orangutan jaw, stained brown to look old.
spotlights.story_md: In 1912, a solicitor and amateur collector, **Charles Dawson**, and the Natural History Museum's Arthur Smith Woodward announced the *first Englishman*, found in a gravel pit at Piltdown in Sussex. It had a large human braincase and an ape's jaw, just what experts expected: brain first, the rest later. For 40 years it distorted the field and helped people dismiss the real Taung Child. In 1953, fluorine tests by Kenneth Oakley and analysis by Joseph Weiner and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark exposed it: a medieval human skull and an orangutan jaw, with the teeth filed down. A 2016 study pointed to Dawson as the forger.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous fraud in science, and a warning about seeing what you expect.
spotlights.memory_hook: A big brain, a filed orangutan jaw and 40 years of belief.

spotlights.name: The Old Man of La Chapelle
spotlights.spot_it: The skull behind the image of the shuffling, bent-kneed caveman.
spotlights.story_md: In 1908 three priests excavating near La Chapelle-aux-Saints in France found a nearly complete Neanderthal skeleton in a pit. The palaeontologist **Marcellin Boule** studied it and reconstructed a creature with bent knees, a forward-thrust head and a stooped gait, which became the cartoon caveman. In 1957 a re-examination showed the man had been old and severely arthritic, with almost no teeth left. Healthy Neanderthals stood upright. Their brains were on average as large as ours or larger. That he lived so long without teeth suggests others may have helped him eat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It created the brute stereotype that took half a century to undo.
spotlights.memory_hook: An arthritic grandfather mistaken for a whole species.

spotlights.name: Out of Africa versus multiregional
spotlights.spot_it: The great argument, and why both sides were partly right.
spotlights.story_md: In the 1980s, the field split. **Chris Stringer** and others argued for a recent African origin: *Homo sapiens* arose in Africa and replaced other humans. **Milford Wolpoff** and **Alan Thorne** argued for multiregional evolution: humans evolved in place across the Old World, linked by gene flow, from *Homo erectus* ancestors. The genetic evidence came down largely on Stringer's side: well over 90% of non-African ancestry comes from the recent African exit. But the 2010 Neanderthal genome proved some mixing did happen. The current picture is called *leaky replacement*: mostly replacement, with a few per cent absorbed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a fierce scientific debate can resolve into a more interesting middle.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mostly out of Africa, with a little leakage.

sections.title: What is new in 2025 and 2026
sections.intro_md:
The field is moving faster than at any time in its history, mostly because of proteins and DNA pulled from bones, teeth, tooth plaque and cave dirt. In 2025 alone, the Denisovans got a skull and a face, the deep roots of the Asian human lineages were pushed back, and Ethiopia produced a new kind of *Australopithecus* living side by side with early *Homo*.

In 2026, the record for the oldest rock art jumped to at least 67,800 years, and a new date of about 1.77 million years for the Yunxian skulls in China clashed with the 2025 study that had placed them near the Denisovan branch. Expect the dates in this lesson to change. The direction of change has been steady for 30 years: older, more mixed, more spread out across Africa and Asia.

spotlights.name: The Yunxian skulls
spotlights.spot_it: Crushed, flattened skulls from a riverbank in Hubei, China.
spotlights.story_md: Two skulls were found at Yunxian in Hubei in 1989 and 1990, and a third in 2022. All were badly crushed. In September 2025 a team including **Chris Stringer** and **Xijun Ni** digitally restored Yunxian 2 and argued that it, at about a million years old, was an early member of the *Homo longi* group that includes the Denisovans, implying that our lineage split from theirs over a million years ago. In February 2026, cosmogenic dating put the site at about **1.77 million years** and called the skulls *Homo erectus*. Both cannot easily be right, which makes this the liveliest fight in the field.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It decides whether the Denisovan and sapiens lines split over a million years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three crushed skulls, two papers, one big argument.

spotlights.name: Ledi-Geraru
spotlights.when: Teeth 2.78 to 2.59 million years old; published August 2025
spotlights.spot_it: Badlands in Ethiopia's Afar region where early Homo and a new Australopithecus lived side by side.
spotlights.story_md: In 2013 a jaw found at Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia, about 2.8 million years old, became the oldest known member of our genus, *Homo*. In August 2025, the team, including **Brian Villmoare** and Kaye Reed, reported more teeth: *Homo* at 2.78 and 2.59 million years, and *Australopithecus* at 2.63 million years that does not match Lucy's species or any other named one. So two kinds of human-like animals lived in the same landscape at the same time, a few hundred thousand years after Lucy's kind disappeared. The site lies in the same Afar region where Lucy was found, a short drive from Hadar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It confirms that early Homo did not replace Australopithecus in a single tidy step.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two lineages, one landscape, 2.6 million years ago.

sections.title: Recap: the story in one breath
sections.intro_md:
Our species formed in Africa over hundreds of thousands of years, from linked populations spread from Morocco to the Cape; the oldest fossils, at Jebel Irhoud, are about 315,000 years old. Earlier human species had left Africa as early as 1.8 million years ago, and *Homo sapiens* itself made several early exits that mostly faded out. The expansion that worked began roughly 60,000 to 50,000 years ago. Its people met Neanderthals and Denisovans, mixed with them, and carried their genes to India, Tibet, Papua and the Americas. They painted caves in Sulawesi and France, crossed seas to Australia and walked a land bridge that has since drowned.

Three tests to carry: Who were the other humans? (Neanderthals, Denisovans, floresiensis, luzonensis, naledi.) What is the evidence? (Fossils, artefacts, DNA, each with its own clock.) What is still argued? (Exact dates, routes, and how often the branches met.)

best_facts.fact: The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils were found by baryte miners in Morocco in 1961, and in 2017 they were dated to about 315,000 years, more than 100,000 years older than expected.
best_facts.why_surprising: The cradle of our species turned up in Africa's far north-west, not the East African Rift.

best_facts.fact: A girl who lived about 90,000 years ago in a Siberian cave had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. She is known from a single bone fragment about 2 cm long.
best_facts.why_surprising: A first-generation hybrid of two human species, found among only a handful of ancient genomes.

best_facts.fact: About half of all South Asians carry a block of Neanderthal DNA that was found in 2020 to be the biggest genetic risk factor for severe COVID-19.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 50,000-year-old encounter showed up in hospital wards.

best_facts.fact: The oldest dated rock art made by our species is not in France but on Muna Island in Indonesia: a hand stencil at least 67,800 years old.
best_facts.why_surprising: Europe's famous caves are about 30,000 years younger.

best_facts.fact: The Neanderthal valley is named after a hymn writer, Joachim Neander, whose surname was a Greek rendering of Neumann, meaning new man.
best_facts.why_surprising: The first old human species was found in the valley of the new man.

best_facts.fact: The Laetoli footprints were found because a scientist dodging elephant dung, thrown in a camp game, fell onto a surface covered in fossil tracks.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the great finds of human evolution started with a dung fight.

best_facts.fact: The Taung Child, the first early human found in Africa, was probably killed by an eagle: its eye sockets carry talon marks like those left by modern crowned eagles.
best_facts.why_surprising: Our ancestors were sometimes prey for birds.

best_facts.fact: Tibetans owe part of their ability to live at high altitude to a version of the EPAS1 gene inherited from Denisovans.
best_facts.why_surprising: An extinct human group still helps living people breathe.

best_facts.fact: Svante Pääbo, who read the Neanderthal genome, won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; his father, Sune Bergström, won the same prize in 1982.
best_facts.why_surprising: Two Nobels in one family, 40 years apart, for different work.

best_facts.fact: The Harbin skull, the first skull firmly linked to the Denisovans, was reportedly hidden in a well in 1933 and only handed to scientists in 2018. DNA from the plaque on its one tooth identified it.
best_facts.why_surprising: A species known from a pinky bone got its face from dental plaque.

best_facts.fact: Oase 1, a man who lived in Romania about 40,000 years ago, had a Neanderthal ancestor only four to six generations back.
best_facts.why_surprising: His great-great-great-grandparent was from another human species.

best_facts.fact: Handaxes at Attirampakkam near Chennai have been dated to about 1.5 million years, long before Homo sapiens existed.
best_facts.why_surprising: India was home to tool-making humans over a million years before our species.

best_facts.fact: Piltdown Man, Britain's first Englishman, was a medieval human skull with an orangutan jaw whose teeth had been filed down. It fooled experts for about 40 years.
best_facts.why_surprising: The fake fitted what experts expected, so they believed it.

best_facts.fact: Chimpanzees from a single region of Africa carry more genetic diversity than all 8 billion humans put together.
best_facts.why_surprising: Humans look varied but are genetically young and uniform.

best_facts.fact: Ancient footprints at White Sands in New Mexico, about 23,000 to 21,000 years old, were mostly made by teenagers and children.
best_facts.why_surprising: The first known Americans in the footprint record were kids.

best_facts.fact: Indians carry the largest variety of population-specific Neanderthal DNA segments of any group studied, according to a 2025 study of 2,762 genomes.
best_facts.why_surprising: India is a library of Neanderthal genes.

side_dish.title: When did humans start talking?
side_dish.body_md:
Words leave no fossils, so the origin of language is one of the hardest questions in science. The clues are indirect.

**Anatomy.** Speech needs a low larynx and a small, horseshoe-shaped bone in the throat called the **hyoid**, which anchors the tongue. In 1983 excavators at Kebara Cave in Israel found the hyoid of a Neanderthal, Kebara 2, about 60,000 years old. It is almost identical to ours.

**Genes.** A gene called **FOXP2** is needed for fine control of the mouth and face; a family in London with a broken copy struggled to speak. In 2007, Pääbo's team found that Neanderthals carried the same version as modern humans.

**Behaviour.** Symbols such as the engraved ochre of Blombos Cave, 75,000 years ago, suggest people who could hold shared meanings, and that is hard to imagine without language.

Today about 7,000 languages are spoken. Some linguists have argued that the click languages of southern Africa preserve very old sounds, and a 2011 study claimed that the number of distinct sounds in a language falls with distance from Africa, mirroring the genetic pattern. Both ideas are contested. What is clear is that language is old, probably older than our species, and that the cousins we met on the way out of Africa may have been able to talk back.

offline_task.title: Make a 67,000-year-old picture
offline_task.body_md:
The oldest known art by our species is a hand stencil. Make one tonight.

1. Put a sheet of paper on newspaper. Lay your hand flat on it, fingers spread.
2. Dip an old toothbrush in watercolour, ink or diluted coffee. Hold it above your hand and rub your thumb across the bristles to spray a fine mist around your fingers. A straw works too: blow across the top of a straw dipped in paint, the way stencils in Sulawesi and Spain were made with a mouthful of pigment.
3. Lift your hand. You have a negative hand, the same image people left in caves on Muna Island at least 67,800 years ago.
4. Try a second one with one finger pointing, like a stencil at Liang Metanduno.

Then ask the question archaeologists ask: what would make you want to leave your hand on a cave wall? Write one line of an answer on the back.
